claim: Transport of synaptic vesicles (SVs) in nerve terminals is thought to play essential roles in maintenance of neurotransmission.
source: Transport of synaptic vesicles (SVs) in nerve terminals is thought to play essential roles in maintenance of neurotransmission.
evidence: This is a statement from the abstract that reflects established scientific understanding about SV transport.

claim: SV movements in giant calyceal terminals were faster than in small hippocampal terminals.
source: Compared with small hippocampal terminals, SV movements in giant calyceal terminals were faster, longer and kinetically more heterogeneous.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data comparing the two terminal types presented in the manuscript.

claim: SV movements in giant calyceal terminals were longer than in small hippocampal terminals.
source: Compared with small hippocampal terminals, SV movements in giant calyceal terminals were faster, longer and kinetically more heterogeneous.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data comparing trajectory lengths between terminal types.

claim: SV movements in giant calyceal terminals were kinetically more heterogeneous than in small hippocampal terminals.
source: Compared with small hippocampal terminals, SV movements in giant calyceal terminals were faster, longer and kinetically more heterogeneous.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing variation in movement patterns.

claim: Morphological maturation of giant calyceal terminals was associated with an overall reduction in SV mobility.
source: Morphological maturation of giant calyceal terminals was associated with an overall reduction in SV mobility and displacement heterogeneity.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data comparing immature and mature terminals.

claim: Morphological maturation of giant calyceal terminals was associated with a reduction in displacement heterogeneity.
source: Morphological maturation of giant calyceal terminals was associated with an overall reduction in SV mobility and displacement heterogeneity.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data comparing immature and mature terminals.

claim: SVs over-expressing vesicular glutamate transporter 1 (VGLUT1) showed higher mobility than VGLUT2-expressing SVs.
source: At the molecular level, SVs over-expressing vesicular glutamate transporter 1 (VGLUT1) showed higher mobility than VGLUT2-expressing SVs.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data comparing SVs expressing different VGLUT subtypes.

claim: Pharmacological disruption of the presynaptic microtubule network preferentially reduced long directional movements of SVs between release sites.
source: Pharmacological disruption of the presynaptic microtubule network preferentially reduced long directional movements of SVs between release sites.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data using nocodazole treatment.

claim: Synaptic stimulation appeared to recruit SVs to active zones without significantly altering their mobility.
source: Functionally, synaptic stimulation appeared to recruit SVs to active zones without significantly altering their mobility.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from stimulation experiments.

claim: The morphological features of nerve terminals are key elements determining vesicular dynamics and movements in central synapses.
source: Hence, the morphological features of nerve terminals and the molecular signature of vesicles are key elements determining vesicular dynamics and movements in central synapses.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented in the study.

claim: The molecular signature of vesicles are key elements determining vesicular dynamics and movements in central synapses.
source: Hence, the morphological features of nerve terminals and the molecular signature of vesicles are key elements determining vesicular dynamics and movements in central synapses.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented in the study.

claim: After exocytosis, SVs are retrieved by endocytosis, refilled with neurotransmitter, and transported to release sites to be reused.
source: After exocytosis, SVs are retrieved by endocytosis, refilled with neurotransmitter, and transported to release sites to be reused (Heuser and Reese, 1973).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Cellular and molecular mechanisms of exocytosis and endocytosis have been extensively studied.
source: Although cellular and molecular mechanisms of exocytosis and endocytosis have been extensively studied (Sudhof, 2004; Jahn and Fasshauer, 2012), movements of SVs between endocytosis and exocytosis are least understood.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Movements of SVs between endocytosis and exocytosis are least understood.
source: Although cellular and molecular mechanisms of exocytosis and endocytosis have been extensively studied (Sudhof, 2004; Jahn and Fasshauer, 2012), movements of SVs between endocytosis and exocytosis are least understood.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of knowledge in the field.

claim: Previous studies have reported a wide range of SV mobility, several orders of magnitude different in their diffusion coefficient (D), between different types or even in the same type of presynaptic terminal.
source: Previous studies have reported a wide range of SV mobility, several orders of magnitude different in their diffusion coefficient (D), between different types or even in the same type of presynaptic terminal (Holt et al., 2004; Rea et al., 2004; Jordan et al., 2005; Westphal et al., 2008; Kamin et al., 2010; Lee et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous work.

claim: SVs display low mobility at both hippocampal and neuromuscular synapses.
source: Within nerve terminals, at both hippocampal and neuromuscular synapses, SVs reportedly display low mobility (Lee et al., 2012; Lemke and Klingauf, 2005; Gaffield and Betz, 2007), whereas SVs traveling across distant hippocampal presynaptic boutons show higher mobility (Lee et al., 2012; Darcy et al., 2006; Fernandez-Alfonso and Ryan, 2008; Staras et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: SVs traveling across distant hippocampal presynaptic boutons show higher mobility.
source: Within nerve terminals, at both hippocampal and neuromuscular synapses, SVs reportedly display low mobility (Lee et al., 2012; Lemke and Klingauf, 2005; Gaffield and Betz, 2007), whereas SVs traveling across distant hippocampal presynaptic boutons show higher mobility (Lee et al., 2012; Darcy et al., 2006; Fernandez-Alfonso and Ryan, 2008; Staras et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: It is controversial whether stimulation can affect SV mobility.
source: It is also controversial whether stimulation can affect SV mobility (Gaffield et al., 2006; Peng et al., 2012) or not (Betz and Bewick, 1992; Westphal et al., 2008; Kamin et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to conflicting previous work.

claim: Synapsin-1 has long been identified as a tether anchoring and releasing SVs in a phosphorylation-dependent manner.
source: Synapsin-1 has long been identified as a tether anchoring and releasing SVs in a phosphorylation-dependent manner (Llinás et al., 1985) and is thought to regulate SV mobility in various nerve terminals (Jordan et al., 2005; Gaffield et al., 2006; Rothman et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Synapsin-1 is thought to regulate SV mobility in various nerve terminals.
source: Synapsin-1 has long been identified as a tether anchoring and releasing SVs in a phosphorylation-dependent manner (Llinás et al., 1985) and is thought to regulate SV mobility in various nerve terminals (Jordan et al., 2005; Gaffield et al., 2006; Rothman et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: Actin network has been implicated in the regulation of fast trafficking of SVs between synaptic sites in central synapses.
source: Actin network has also been implicated in the regulation of fast trafficking of SVs between synaptic sites in central synapses (Darcy et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: The roles of microtubules and their associated molecular motors are well established for axonal transport.
source: The roles of another cytosketal element, microtubules (MTs) and their associated molecular motors are well established for axonal transport (Hirokawa et al., 2009, 2010), but their contribution in the regulation of SV dynamics within nerve terminals remains to be elucidated.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The contribution of microtubules in the regulation of SV dynamics within nerve terminals remains to be elucidated.
source: The roles of another cytosketal element, microtubules (MTs) and their associated molecular motors are well established for axonal transport (Hirokawa et al., 2009, 2010), but their contribution in the regulation of SV dynamics within nerve terminals remains to be elucidated.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of knowledge in the field.

claim: Mechanical factors such as membrane tensions are proposed to promote accumulation of SVs in nerve terminals.
source: Mechanical factors such as membrane tensions are proposed to promote accumulation of SVs in nerve terminals (Siechen et al., 2009) or to increase their mobility (Ahmed et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Mechanical factors such as membrane tensions are proposed to increase SV mobility.
source: Mechanical factors such as membrane tensions are proposed to promote accumulation of SVs in nerve terminals (Siechen et al., 2009) or to increase their mobility (Ahmed et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Experimentally constrained models suggested that physical determinants such as hydrodynamic interaction and vesicle collision influence SV movements in presynaptic terminals.
source: More recently, experimentally constrained models suggested that physical determinants such as hydrodynamic interaction and vesicle collision influence SV movements in presynaptic terminals (Rothman et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Biological factors and mechanisms underlying the diversity of SV mobility in nerve terminals remain poorly understood.
source: However, biological factors and mechanisms underlying the diversity of SV mobility in nerve terminals remain poorly understood.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of knowledge in the field.

claim: Imaging studies of SV mobility in mammalian central synapses have been restricted to small hippocampal synapses.
source: In mammalian central synapses, imaging studies of SV mobility have been restricted to small hippocampal synapses.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of research in the field.

claim: The study used newly developed giant glutamatergic synapses formed in primary culture between mouse auditory brainstem neurons.
source: Here, by taking advantage of our newly developed giant glutamatergic synapses formed in primary culture between mouse auditory brainstem neurons (Dimitrov et al., 2016), we visualized SVs using real-time confocal microscopy, and analyzed their movements by automatically tracking large populations of fluorescently labelled vesicles within presynaptic terminals.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: The study analyzed more than 35,000 vesicle trajectories.
source: We then performed spatio-temporal analyses of more than 35,000 vesicle trajectories to quantify their intrinsic dynamic properties (i.e. maximum speed and track length), their modalities of displacement (i.e. diffusive or active motions), and their overall mobility (i.e. diffusion coefficient).
evidence: This is a statement about the data collected in the study.

claim: The average number of labeled vesicles per terminal significantly increased with length of exposure to Q655-Syt2, reaching ~1500 SVs per terminal after 16 hr.
source: The average number of labeled vesicles per terminal significantly increased with length of exposure to Q655-Syt2, reaching ~1500 SVs per terminal after 16 hr (Figure 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The use of synaptotagmin-2 antibody significantly increased the efficiency of SV labeling, in comparison to quantum dots only.
source: The use of synaptotagmin-2 antibody significantly increased the efficiency of SV labeling, in comparison to quantum dots only (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A,B.

claim: The fluorescence intensity distribution in 150 nm confocal spots for Q655-Syt2-labeled SVs was similar to the one from 40 nm FITC-beads.
source: The fluorescence intensity distribution in 150 nm confocal spots for Q655-Syt2-labeled SVs was similar to the one from 40 nm FITC-beads (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C), suggesting single vesicle detection in our tracking experiments.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: The fluorescence intensity distribution suggests single vesicle detection in the tracking experiments.
source: The fluorescence intensity distribution in 150 nm confocal spots for Q655-Syt2-labeled SVs was similar to the one from 40 nm FITC-beads (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C), suggesting single vesicle detection in our tracking experiments.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the fluorescence intensity data.

claim: The diffusion coefficient (D) calculated from the mean square displacement (MSD) curves of trajectories identified with the autoregressive algorithm was seven times greater than that calculated from the MSD determined by the Brownian algorithm.
source: The diffusion coefficient (D), calculated from the mean square displacement (MSD) curves of trajectories identified with the autoregressive algorithm (D = 0.065 ± 0.004 µm2/s), was seven times greater than that calculated from the MSD determined by the Brownian algorithm (D = 0.009 ± 0.001 µm2/s).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data comparing two tracking algorithms.

claim: Vesicle mobility could be underestimated by analysis based solely on the Brownian motion algorithm.
source: This suggests that vesicle mobility could be underestimated by analysis based solely on the Brownian motion algorithm (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the comparison of tracking algorithms.

claim: Aldehyde fixation of labeled giant terminals lowered SV mobility to the level of mobility observed for 40 nm fluorescent polystyrene beads adsorbed onto glass coverslips.
source: Aldehyde fixation of labeled giant terminals lowered SV mobility (D = 0.008 ± 0.001 µm2/s) to the level of mobility observed for 40 nm fluorescent polystyrene beads adsorbed onto glass coverslips (D = 0.008 ± 0.001 µm2/s), indicating that the signal-to-noise ratio in our tracking experiments was ~8 (Figure 1E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data comparing fixed samples to beads.

claim: The signal-to-noise ratio in the tracking experiments was ~8.
source: Aldehyde fixation of labeled giant terminals lowered SV mobility (D = 0.008 ± 0.001 µm2/s) to the level of mobility observed for 40 nm fluorescent polystyrene beads adsorbed onto glass coverslips (D = 0.008 ± 0.001 µm2/s), indicating that the signal-to-noise ratio in our tracking experiments was ~8 (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is calculated from the comparison of mobile and fixed vesicle data.

claim: Stimulation with 65 mM KCl induced an 80% decrease in the fluorescence intensity of C5E-Syt2-loaded vesicles.
source: Stimulation with 65 mM KCl induced an 80% decrease in the fluorescence intensity of C5E-Syt2-loaded vesicles, showing that a large proportion of labeled SVs underwent exocytosis (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2B.

claim: A large proportion of labeled SVs underwent exocytosis upon KCl stimulation.
source: Stimulation with 65 mM KCl induced an 80% decrease in the fluorescence intensity of C5E-Syt2-loaded vesicles, showing that a large proportion of labeled SVs underwent exocytosis (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the fluorescence decrease data.

claim: Diffusion coefficients of SVs labeled with Qdots (Q655 and Q585) or with C5E were similar.
source: Furthermore, diffusion coefficients of SVs labeled with Qdots (Q655 and Q585) or with C5E were similar (Figure 1E), indicating that labeling methods did not affect their dynamic or functional properties.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Labeling methods did not affect SV dynamic or functional properties.
source: Furthermore, diffusion coefficients of SVs labeled with Qdots (Q655 and Q585) or with C5E were similar (Figure 1E), indicating that labeling methods did not affect their dynamic or functional properties.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the similarity of diffusion coefficients.

claim: In presynaptic swellings, ~40% of SVs were mobile with T1/2 = 13.2 ± 1.1 s and a calculated diffusion coefficient of 0.029 ± 0.007 µm2/s.
source: Data pooled from three different terminals showed that in presynaptic swellings, ~40% of SVs were mobile (T1/2 = 13.2 ± 1.1 s) with a calculated diffusion coefficient (Axelrod et al., 1976) of 0.029 ± 0.007 µm2/s, whereas in finger-like processes, ~80% of SVs were mobile (T1/2 = 6.3 ± 0.7 s) with a diffusion coefficient of 0.061 ± 0.007 µm2/s.
evidence: This claim is supported by FRAP experimental data.

claim: In finger-like processes, ~80% of SVs were mobile with T1/2 = 6.3 ± 0.7 s and a diffusion coefficient of 0.061 ± 0.007 µm2/s.
source: Data pooled from three different terminals showed that in presynaptic swellings, ~40% of SVs were mobile (T1/2 = 13.2 ± 1.1 s) with a calculated diffusion coefficient (Axelrod et al., 1976) of 0.029 ± 0.007 µm2/s, whereas in finger-like processes, ~80% of SVs were mobile (T1/2 = 6.3 ± 0.7 s) with a diffusion coefficient of 0.061 ± 0.007 µm2/s.
evidence: This claim is supported by FRAP experimental data.

claim: The mobility of newly retrieved SVs in hippocampal synapses is highest after endocytosis and gradually decreases thereafter.
source: In addition, it has been reported that the mobility of newly retrieved SVs in hippocampal synapses is highest after endocytosis and gradually decreases thereafter (Kamin et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: One hour after the second loading, SVs newly labeled with Q585-Syt2 remained in restricted regions of the terminal, not mixing with previously retrieved Q655-Syt2-labeled vesicles.
source: One hour after the second loading, SVs newly labeled with Q585-Syt2 remained in restricted regions of the terminal, not mixing with previously retrieved Q655-Syt2-labeled vesicles (Pearson co-localization index, p=0.087 ± 0.06; Figure 1—figure supplement 3B), and showed relatively low mobility (D = 0.045 ± 0.001 µm2/s).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3B.

claim: Newly labeled SVs showed relatively low mobility one hour after loading (D = 0.045 ± 0.001 µm2/s).
source: One hour after the second loading, SVs newly labeled with Q585-Syt2 remained in restricted regions of the terminal, not mixing with previously retrieved Q655-Syt2-labeled vesicles (Pearson co-localization index, p=0.087 ± 0.06; Figure 1—figure supplement 3B), and showed relatively low mobility (D = 0.045 ± 0.001 µm2/s).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data.

claim: Two to three hours after the second loading, SVs labeled with Q585-Syt2 increased their mobility (D = 0.066 ± 0.005 µm2/s after 3 hr).
source: Two to three hours after the second loading, SVs labeled with Q585-Syt2 increased their mobility (D = 0.066 ± 0.005 µm2/s after 3 hr; Figure 1—figure supplement 3C,D) and gradually mixed with the pre-existing pool of SVs labeled with Q655-Syt2 (p=0.266 ± 0.035; Figure 1—figure supplement 3A,E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3C,D.

claim: SVs labeled with Q585-Syt2 gradually mixed with the pre-existing pool of SVs labeled with Q655-Syt2 after 2-3 hours.
source: Two to three hours after the second loading, SVs labeled with Q585-Syt2 increased their mobility (D = 0.066 ± 0.005 µm2/s after 3 hr; Figure 1—figure supplement 3C,D) and gradually mixed with the pre-existing pool of SVs labeled with Q655-Syt2 (p=0.266 ± 0.035; Figure 1—figure supplement 3A,E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3A,E.

claim: Of all SVs examined in 12 giant terminals, 61% had short trajectories and slow motility.
source: Of all SVs examined in 12 giant terminals, 61% had short trajectories and slow motility, whereas 39% had long (up to 6 µm) and fast (up to 0.8 µm/s) directional movements (Figure 2C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: 39% of SVs had long (up to 6 µm) and fast (up to 0.8 µm/s) directional movements.
source: Of all SVs examined in 12 giant terminals, 61% had short trajectories and slow motility, whereas 39% had long (up to 6 µm) and fast (up to 0.8 µm/s) directional movements (Figure 2C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: ~20% of labeled SVs move actively in calyceal terminals.
source: We categorized displacement modalities of SVs into two groups: one with diffusive motion and the other with active (facilitated or impeded displacements) motion (Figure 2—figure supplement 2C), and found that ~20% of labeled SVs move actively in calyceal terminals (Figure 2D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: At mouse hippocampal synapses, the phosphatase inhibitor okadaic acid (OA) dramatically increases SV mobility.
source: At mouse hippocampal synapses (Kraszewski et al., 1995; Jordan et al., 2005) and frog neuromuscular junctions (Betz and Henkel, 1994; Gaffield et al., 2006), the phosphatase inhibitor, okadaic acid (OA) dramatically increases SV mobility.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: At frog neuromuscular junctions, the phosphatase inhibitor okadaic acid (OA) dramatically increases SV mobility.
source: At mouse hippocampal synapses (Kraszewski et al., 1995; Jordan et al., 2005) and frog neuromuscular junctions (Betz and Henkel, 1994; Gaffield et al., 2006), the phosphatase inhibitor, okadaic acid (OA) dramatically increases SV mobility.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: At giant calyceal terminals, OA increased SV mobility by ~43% (from D = 0.065 ± 0.004 µm2/s to 0.093 ± 0.008 µm2/s).
source: At giant calyceal terminals, OA increased SV mobility by ~43% (from D = 0.065 ± 0.004 µm2/s to 0.093 ± 0.008 µm2/s, Figure 2E), a significant, but moderate increase compared with those reported previously.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: SV mobility was ~1.4 times higher in finger-like processes (D = 0.059 ± 0.004 µm2/s) than in swellings (D = 0.044 ± 0.003 µm2/s).
source: As suggested from FRAP experiments (Figure 1—figure supplement 3D,E), SV mobility was ~1.4 times higher in finger-like processes (D = 0.059 ± 0.004 µm2/s) than in swellings (D = 0.044 ± 0.003 µm2/s, Figure 2—figure supplement 2D,E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2D,E.

claim: OA enhanced SV mobility ~1.4 times in both swellings and finger-like regions.
source: Consistently, OA also enhanced SV mobility ~1.4 times in both regions (Figure 2—figure supplement 2E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2E.

claim: Lowering the temperature from physiological (37°C) to non-physiological (25°C) conditions decreased the diffusion coefficient of SVs by ~30% (from D = 0.065 ± 0.004 µm2/s to D = 0.046 ± 0.003 µm2/s).
source: Lowering the temperature from physiological (37°C) to non-physiological (25°C) conditions decreased the diffusion coefficient of SVs by ~30% (from D = 0.065 ± 0.004 µm2/s to D = 0.046 ± 0.003 µm2/s, Figure 2E), with a temperature coefficient (Q10) of 1.6, indicating that SV movements were moderately more temperature-dependent than diffusion (Q10 = 1.3).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: SV movements have a temperature coefficient (Q10) of 1.6.
source: Lowering the temperature from physiological (37°C) to non-physiological (25°C) conditions decreased the diffusion coefficient of SVs by ~30% (from D = 0.065 ± 0.004 µm2/s to D = 0.046 ± 0.003 µm2/s, Figure 2E), with a temperature coefficient (Q10) of 1.6, indicating that SV movements were moderately more temperature-dependent than diffusion (Q10 = 1.3).
evidence: This is calculated from the temperature-dependent data.

claim: SV movements were moderately more temperature-dependent than diffusion (Q10 = 1.3).
source: Lowering the temperature from physiological (37°C) to non-physiological (25°C) conditions decreased the diffusion coefficient of SVs by ~30% (from D = 0.065 ± 0.004 µm2/s to D = 0.046 ± 0.003 µm2/s, Figure 2E), with a temperature coefficient (Q10) of 1.6, indicating that SV movements were moderately more temperature-dependent than diffusion (Q10 = 1.3).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the comparison of Q10 values.

claim: Under resting conditions, 25% of labeled vesicles move outward toward the postsynaptic cell.
source: We further analyzed SV movements and distributions in 3D within presynaptic terminals and found that under resting conditions, 25% of labeled vesicles move outward toward the postsynaptic cell, 14% move inward, and 35% move laterally near the synaptic cleft (Figure 2—figure supplement 2F,G).
evidence: This claim is supported by 3D tracking data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2F,G.

claim: Under resting conditions, 14% of labeled vesicles move inward.
source: We further analyzed SV movements and distributions in 3D within presynaptic terminals and found that under resting conditions, 25% of labeled vesicles move outward toward the postsynaptic cell, 14% move inward, and 35% move laterally near the synaptic cleft (Figure 2—figure supplement 2F,G).
evidence: This claim is supported by 3D tracking data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2F,G.

claim: Under resting conditions, 35% of labeled vesicles move laterally near the synaptic cleft.
source: We further analyzed SV movements and distributions in 3D within presynaptic terminals and found that under resting conditions, 25% of labeled vesicles move outward toward the postsynaptic cell, 14% move inward, and 35% move laterally near the synaptic cleft (Figure 2—figure supplement 2F,G).
evidence: This claim is supported by 3D tracking data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2F,G.

claim: Trajectory proportion and diffusion coefficient were similar between 2D or 3D tracking.
source: Trajectory proportion and diffusion coefficient were similar between 2D or 3D tracking (Figure 2—figure supplement 2H), suggesting a minimum bias in our tracking method cause by movements of different SV in and out of the focal plan.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2H.

claim: The similarity between 2D and 3D tracking suggests a minimum bias in the tracking method caused by movements of different SV in and out of the focal plane.
source: Trajectory proportion and diffusion coefficient were similar between 2D or 3D tracking (Figure 2—figure supplement 2H), suggesting a minimum bias in our tracking method cause by movements of different SV in and out of the focal plan.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the similarity of 2D and 3D tracking data.

claim: The diffusion coefficient of SVs in resting hippocampal boutons was 0.024 ± 0.003 µm2/s.
source: The diffusion coefficient of SVs in resting hippocampal boutons was 0.024 ± 0.003 µm2/s (Figure 3E), ~3 times lower than that in giant calyceal terminals (D = 0.065 ± 0.004 µm2/s, Figure 2E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3E.

claim: The diffusion coefficient of SVs in hippocampal boutons is ~3 times lower than that in giant calyceal terminals.
source: The diffusion coefficient of SVs in resting hippocampal boutons was 0.024 ± 0.003 µm2/s (Figure 3E), ~3 times lower than that in giant calyceal terminals (D = 0.065 ± 0.004 µm2/s, Figure 2E).
evidence: This is a comparison of experimental data from two terminal types.

claim: No differences in D values, calculated using Brownian motion analysis, were observed between hippocampal (D = 0.009 ± 0.001 µm2/s) and calyceal (D = 0.009 ± 0.001 µm2/s) terminals.
source: No differences in D values, calculated using Brownian motion analysis, were observed between hippocampal (D = 0.009 ± 0.001 µm2/s, Figure 3E) and calyceal (D = 0.009 ± 0.001 µm2/s, Figure 2E) terminals.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 2E and 3E.

claim: The size of calyceal swellings was about twice that of hippocampal boutons.
source: Although the size of calyceal swellings was about twice that of hippocampal boutons (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B), when SV movements were compared between swellings and boutons having similar areas, mobility of SVs in swellings was consistently ~2-fold higher than that in boutons (Figure 3F).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: When SV movements were compared between swellings and boutons having similar areas, mobility of SVs in swellings was consistently ~2-fold higher than that in boutons.
source: Although the size of calyceal swellings was about twice that of hippocampal boutons (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B), when SV movements were compared between swellings and boutons having similar areas, mobility of SVs in swellings was consistently ~2-fold higher than that in boutons (Figure 3F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: Within calyceal terminals, SV mobility increased with the size of the swellings (r = 0.85).
source: Within calyceal terminals, SV mobility increased with the size of the swellings (r = 0.85), whereas there was no positive correlation (r = −0.05) between the size of boutons and SV mobility in hippocampal terminals.
evidence: This claim is supported by correlation analysis of experimental data.

claim: There was no positive correlation (r = −0.05) between the size of boutons and SV mobility in hippocampal terminals.
source: Within calyceal terminals, SV mobility increased with the size of the swellings (r = 0.85), whereas there was no positive correlation (r = −0.05) between the size of boutons and SV mobility in hippocampal terminals.
evidence: This claim is supported by correlation analysis of experimental data.

claim: Giant calyceal terminals in culture undergo significant morphological rearrangements and functional maturation.
source: As at the developing calyx of Held, giant calyceal terminals in culture undergo significant morphological rearrangements and functional maturation, which were initially classified into four stages (Dimitrov et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: During morphological maturation of synapses, the volume and surface area of presynaptic terminals increased gradually.
source: During morphological maturation of synapses, the volume and surface area of presynaptic terminals (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A,B), as well as the number of labeled vesicles (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C) increased gradually.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A,B.

claim: During morphological maturation of synapses, the number of labeled vesicles increased gradually.
source: During morphological maturation of synapses, the volume and surface area of presynaptic terminals (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A,B), as well as the number of labeled vesicles (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C) increased gradually.
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Immature terminals were characterized by prominent finger-like processes and presynaptic volumes below 1000 µm3.
source: Immature terminals were characterized by prominent finger-like processes and presynaptic volumes below 1000 µm3, whereas mature terminals were composed of numerous swellings interconnected with finger-like branches and presynaptic volumes above 1000 µm3.
evidence: This is a description of the morphological characteristics used to categorize terminals.

claim: Mature terminals were composed of numerous swellings interconnected with finger-like branches and presynaptic volumes above 1000 µm3.
source: Immature terminals were characterized by prominent finger-like processes and presynaptic volumes below 1000 µm3, whereas mature terminals were composed of numerous swellings interconnected with finger-like branches and presynaptic volumes above 1000 µm3.
evidence: This is a description of the morphological characteristics used to categorize terminals.

claim: SV movements displayed wider heterogeneity in immature (trajectory length, 0–14 µm; maximum speed, 0–1.8 µm/s) than in mature (trajectory length, 0–9 µm; maximum speed, 0–1.4 µm/s) terminals.
source: SV movements displayed wider heterogeneity in immature (trajectory length, 0–14 µm; maximum speed, 0–1.8 µm/s) than in mature (trajectory length, 0–9 µm; maximum speed, 0–1.4 µm/s) terminals (Figure 4C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Morphological maturation of terminals significantly reduced the length (from 6.83 ± 0.46 µm to 5.57 ± 0.07 µm) and speed (from 0.82 ± 0.02 µm/s to 0.74 ± 0.02 µm/s) of SVs with long (L) trajectories.
source: The distribution of trajectories according to their maximum speed and length from nine immature terminals and nine mature terminals showed that morphological maturation of terminals significantly reduced the length (from 6.83 ± 0.46 µm to 5.57 ± 0.07 µm) and speed (from 0.82 ± 0.02 µm/s to 0.74 ± 0.02 µm/s) of SVs with long (L) trajectories (Figure 4D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: The proportion of slow and short vesicles movements increased from immature (50%) to mature (70%) terminals.
source: The proportion of slow and short vesicles movements increased from immature (50%) to mature (70%) terminals, whereas fast, long directional movements decreased from 50% to 30% during morphological maturation of terminals (Figure 4D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Fast, long directional movements decreased from 50% to 30% during morphological maturation of terminals.
source: The proportion of slow and short vesicles movements increased from immature (50%) to mature (70%) terminals, whereas fast, long directional movements decreased from 50% to 30% during morphological maturation of terminals (Figure 4D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: As the calyceal terminal morphology advanced, diffusive motions relative to active directional motions increased by ~1.8 fold.
source: As the calyceal terminal morphology advanced, diffusive motions relative to active directional motions increased by ~1.8 fold (Figure 4E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: SV mobility was significantly reduced after morphological development of calyceal terminals, from immature stage 2 (D = 0.072 ± 0.005 µm2/s) to mature stage 4 (D = 0.052 ± 0.003 µm2/s) terminals.
source: Consistently, SV mobility was significantly reduced after morphological development of calyceal terminals, from immature stage 2 (D = 0.072 ± 0.005 µm2/s) to mature stage 4 (D = 0.052 ± 0.003 µm2/s) terminals (Figure 4F and Figure 4—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4F and Figure 4—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Vesicular glutamate transporters (VGLUTs) transport glutamate into synaptic vesicles.
source: Vesicular glutamate transporters (VGLUTs) transport glutamate into synaptic vesicles (Takamori et al., 2000; Fremeau et al., 2004) and their subtypes VGLUT1 and VGLUT2 reportedly produce different release probabilities (Weston et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: VGLUT1 and VGLUT2 subtypes reportedly produce different release probabilities.
source: Vesicular glutamate transporters (VGLUTs) transport glutamate into synaptic vesicles (Takamori et al., 2000; Fremeau et al., 2004) and their subtypes VGLUT1 and VGLUT2 reportedly produce different release probabilities (Weston et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Giant calyceal terminals in culture express both VGLUT1 and VGLUT2.
source: As giant calyceal terminals in culture express both VGLUT1 and VGLUT2 (Dimitrov et al., 2016), we questioned whether expression of different VGLUT subtypes might affect dynamic properties of SVs in nerve terminals.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work by the authors.

claim: Expression levels of Venus-VGLUT1 and Venus-VGLUT2 were similar after 21 days in culture.
source: After 21 days in culture, expression levels of Venus-VGLUT1 and Venus-VGLUT2, deduced from their fluorescence intensity in the terminals, were similar (Figure 5C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: The generally observed positive correlation between trajectory length and maximum speed was absent in VGLUT2-containing SVs, but was retained in VGLUT1-containing SVs.
source: Surprisingly, the generally observed positive correlation between trajectory length and maximum speed was absent in VGLUT2-containing SVs, but was retained in VGLUT1-containing SVs (Figure 5F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5F.

claim: VGLUT1-containing SVs displayed ~1.6 times (28.9%) more active displacements than VGLUT2-containing SVs (18.2%).
source: VGLUT1-containing SVs displayed ~1.6 times (28.9%) more active displacements than VGLUT2-containing SVs (18.2%, Figure 5G).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5G.

claim: The mobility of vesicles expressing Venus-VGLUT1 (D = 0.072 ± 0.005 µm2/s) was ~1.7 times higher than that of those expressing Venus-VGLUT2 (D = 0.043 ± 0.008 µm2/s).
source: Furthermore, the mobility of vesicles expressing Venus-VGLUT1 (D = 0.072 ± 0.005 µm2/s) was ~1.7 times higher than that of those expressing Venus-VGLUT2 (D = 0.043 ± 0.008 µm2/s, Figure 5H).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5H.

claim: The average diffusion coefficient of Venus-VGLUT1 and Venus-VGLUT2 expressing SVs (D = 0.058 ± 0.006 µm2/s) was similar to those of Q655-Syt2-labeled SVs (D = 0.065 ± 0.004 µm2/s) or C5E-Syt2-labeled SVs (D = 0.063 ± 0.003 µm2/s).
source: Assuming a one-to-one expression ratio in calyceal terminals, the average diffusion coefficient of Venus-VGLUT1 and Venus-VGLUT2 expressing SVs (D = 0.058 ± 0.006 µm2/s) was similar to those of Q655-Syt2-labeled SVs (D = 0.065 ± 0.004 µm2/s) or C5E-Syt2-labeled SVs (D = 0.063 ± 0.003 µm2/s).
evidence: This is a comparison of experimental data from different labeling methods.

claim: Roles of microtubules are well established in axons.
source: Roles of microtubules (MTs) are well established in axons (Conde and Cáceres, 2009), but poorly understood in nerve terminals.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Roles of microtubules are poorly understood in nerve terminals.
source: Roles of microtubules (MTs) are well established in axons (Conde and Cáceres, 2009), but poorly understood in nerve terminals.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of knowledge in the field.

claim: A significant number of vesicles move within giant terminals with speed comparable to that of molecular motors along MTs involved in intracellular organelle transport.
source: Our data indicate that a significant number of vesicles move within giant terminals with speed comparable to that of molecular motors along MTs involved in intracellular organelle transport (Hirokawa et al., 2009, 2010).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data and comparison to known motor speeds.

claim: Synaptic growth involves reorganization of the neuronal cytoskeleton.
source: Synaptic growth involves reorganization of the neuronal cytoskeleton (Roos et al., 2000), which in turn could affect SV mobility.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Giant presynaptic terminals were enriched in de-tyrosinated α-tubulin-containing polymers that interconnect neighboring and distant presynaptic swellings filled with SVs.
source: Immunofluorescence analysis revealed that giant presynaptic terminals were enriched in de-tyrosinated α-tubulin-containing polymers that interconnect neighboring and distant presynaptic swellings filled with SVs (Figure 6A and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 6A and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The molecular motor, KIF1A, was found in calyceal terminals and partially co-localized with the vesicular protein, synaptophysin, within swellings.
source: The molecular motor, KIF1A (Okada et al., 1995), was also found in calyceal terminals and partially co-localized with the vesicular protein, synaptophysin, within swellings (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B,C).
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1B,C.

claim: KIF1A co-localized with VGLUT1-containing SVs in regions that interconnect swellings.
source: KIF1A also co-localized with VGLUT1-containing SVs in regions that interconnect swellings (Figure 6—figure supplement 1D,E), suggesting that KIF1A might carry SVs along MTs within and between swellings.
evidence: This claim is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1D,E.

claim: KIF1A might carry SVs along MTs within and between swellings.
source: KIF1A also co-localized with VGLUT1-containing SVs in regions that interconnect swellings (Figure 6—figure supplement 1D,E), suggesting that KIF1A might carry SVs along MTs within and between swellings.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the co-localization data.

claim: Fluorescence intensity of Silicon-Rhodamine (SiR)-tubulin-containing polymers decreased by ~30% after 90 min incubation with nocodazole.
source: Fluorescence intensity of Silicon-Rhodamine (SiR)-tubulin-containing polymers decreased by ~30% after 90 min incubation with nocodazole (Figure 6B and C), indicating that a significant fraction of MTs in calyceal terminals were depolymerized.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6B and C.

claim: A significant fraction of MTs in calyceal terminals were depolymerized after nocodazole treatment.
source: Fluorescence intensity of Silicon-Rhodamine (SiR)-tubulin-containing polymers decreased by ~30% after 90 min incubation with nocodazole (Figure 6B and C), indicating that a significant fraction of MTs in calyceal terminals were depolymerized.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the decrease in tubulin fluorescence.

claim: Depolymerization of one third of MT networks was sufficient to significantly impair fast, long directional SV movements within terminals.
source: Depolymerization of one third of MT networks was sufficient to significantly impair fast, long directional SV movements within terminals (Figure 6D and E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6D and E.

claim: MT disruption reduced the proportion of SVs with long directional trajectories and concurrently increased the proportion of SVs with short displacements.
source: The distribution of trajectories according to their maximum speed and length (from eight untreated and eight nocodazole-treated terminals) showed that MT disruption reduced the proportion of SVs with long directional trajectories and concurrently increased the proportion of SVs with short displacements (Figure 6F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6F.

claim: The apparently lower mobility observed after nocodazole treatment (D = 0.057 ± 0.004 µm2/s) was not significant compared to controls before treatment (D = 0.066 ± 0.005 µm2/s).
source: However, the apparently lower mobility observed after nocodazole treatment (D = 0.057 ± 0.004 µm2/s) was not significant compared to controls before treatment (D = 0.066 ± 0.005 µm2/s, Figure 6G).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6G.

claim: Disruption of actin network did not affect the movement of SVs between swellings.
source: On the other hand, disruption of actin network, which essentially localized within discreet regions of presynaptic swellings (Figure 6—figure supplement 2A,B), did not affect the movement of SVs between swellings (Figure 6—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2C.

claim: MT depolymerization selectively reduces the maximum speed and the proportion of SVs travelling long distances.
source: These results indicate that MT depolymerization selectively reduces the maximum speed and the proportion of SVs travelling long distances, suggesting a dominant role of MT-based transport for SVs undergoing inter-swelling trafficking in giant terminals.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the nocodazole treatment data.

claim: MT-based transport plays a dominant role for SVs undergoing inter-swelling trafficking in giant terminals.
source: These results indicate that MT depolymerization selectively reduces the maximum speed and the proportion of SVs travelling long distances, suggesting a dominant role of MT-based transport for SVs undergoing inter-swelling trafficking in giant terminals.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the nocodazole treatment data.

claim: KCl stimulation decreased the number of labeled SVs.
source: In giant terminal swellings, KCl stimulation decreased the number of labeled SVs (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B) and redistributed SVs to smaller areas (Figure 1—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2B.

claim: KCl stimulation redistributed SVs to smaller areas.
source: In giant terminal swellings, KCl stimulation decreased the number of labeled SVs (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B) and redistributed SVs to smaller areas (Figure 1—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2C.

claim: Long trajectories markedly decreased while the proportion of intermediate trajectories increased and short trajectories remained unchanged after KCl stimulation.
source: However, long trajectories markedly decreased while the proportion of intermediate trajectories increased and short trajectories remained unchanged (Figure 7D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7D.

claim: SV displacement modalities were unaffected by KCl stimulation.
source: SV displacement modalities were also unaffected by KCl stimulation (Figure 7E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7E.

claim: SV mobility was reduced ~2.7 times (from D = 0.059 ± 0.004 µm2/s to 0.022 ± 0.002 µm2/s) after KCl stimulation.
source: Surprisingly, SV mobility was reduced ~2.7 times (from D = 0.059 ± 0.004 µm2/s to 0.022 ± 0.002 µm2/s) after KCl stimulation (Figure 7F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7F.

claim: The reduction in SV mobility after KCl stimulation was only observed in swelling regions, but not in finger-like regions.
source: However, this reduction was only observed in swelling regions, but not in finger-like regions (Figure 2—figure supplement 2E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2E.

claim: Bath application of hypertonic sucrose solution had no effect on SV trajectories.
source: Bath application of hypertonic sucrose solution had no effect on SV trajectories (Figure 7B), nor on the proportion of long, short, and intermediate movements (Figure 7D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7B and 7D.

claim: Hypertonic sucrose induced a ~2.2-fold decrease in the proportion of active motions (from 14.2% to 6.3%).
source: Interestingly, hypertonic sucrose induced a ~2.2-fold decrease in the proportion of active motions (from 14.2% to 6.3%, Figure 7E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7E.

claim: Hypertonic sucrose had no effect on SV mobility in the RRP.
source: However, hypertonic sucrose had no effect on SV mobility in the RRP (Figure 7F and Figure 2—figure supplement 2E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7F and Figure 2—figure supplement 2E.

claim: Electrical stimulation at 1 Hz induced significant endocytosis.
source: We next stimulated calyceal terminals electrically at 1 Hz. Although this stimulation induced significant endocytosis (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A), SV trajectories (Figure 7B), displacement modalities (Figure 7C), and overall mobility (Figure 7F and Figure 2—figure supplement 2E) remained unchanged.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1A.

claim: SV trajectories, displacement modalities, and overall mobility remained unchanged during 1 Hz electrical stimulation.
source: We next stimulated calyceal terminals electrically at 1 Hz. Although this stimulation induced significant endocytosis (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A), SV trajectories (Figure 7B), displacement modalities (Figure 7C), and overall mobility (Figure 7F and Figure 2—figure supplement 2E) remained unchanged.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figures 7B, 7C, 7F, and Figure 2—figure supplement 2E.

claim: SVs undergoing spontaneous and stimulation-evoked release belong to different pools in presynaptic terminals.
source: It has been postulated that SVs undergoing spontaneous and stimulation-evoked release belong to different pools in presynaptic terminals (Chung et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Electrical stimulation in the presence of C5E-Syt2 significantly increased the number of C5E-loaded vesicles in terminals, as well as their fluorescence intensity.
source: Electrical stimulation in the presence of C5E-Syt2, significantly increased the number of C5E-loaded vesicles in terminals, as well as their fluorescence intensity (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A), as reported previously in KCl-stimulated hippocampal neurons (Kraszewski et al., 1995).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1A and a citation to previous work.

claim: The mobility of SVs loaded upon electrical stimulation (D = 0.052 ± 0.003 µm2/s) was not different from that of those loaded spontaneously for 1 hr before stimulation (D = 0.048 ± 0.005 µm2/s).
source: However, the mobility of SVs loaded upon electrical stimulation (D = 0.052 ± 0.003 µm2/s) was not different from that of those loaded spontaneously for 1 hr before stimulation (D = 0.048 ± 0.005 µm2/s, Figure 7—figure supplement 1B,C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1B,C.

claim: Neither chemical nor electrical stimulation significantly increased SV dynamic properties and mobility in giant calyceal terminals.
source: Thus, while the number of moving vesicles might vary, neither chemical nor electrical stimulation significantly increased their dynamic properties and mobility in giant calyceal terminals.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the stimulation experiments.

claim: During field electrical stimulation at 1 Hz, the proportion of SVs significantly increased by ~1.8 times near release sites (from 21% to 38%).
source: We showed that during field electrical stimulation at 1 Hz, the proportion of SVs significantly increased by ~1.8 times near release sites (from 21% to 38%, Figure 8C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8C.

claim: The mobility of SVs inside (Din = 0.027 ± 0.008 µm2/s) and outside (Dout = 0.044 ± 0.003 µm2/s) of AZs remained largely unaffected during stimulation (Din = 0.024 ± 0.007 µm2/s and Dout = 0.037 ± 0.005 µm2/s).
source: However, the mobility of SVs inside (Din = 0.027 ± 0.008 µm2/s) and outside (Dout = 0.044 ± 0.003 µm2/s) of AZs remained largely unaffected during stimulation (Din = 0.024 ± 0.007 µm2/s and Dout = 0.037 ± 0.005 µm2/s; Figure 8D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8D.

claim: Electrical stimulation recruits SVs to AZs without altering their overall mobility.
source: Thus, our data indicate that electrical stimulation recruits SVs to AZs without altering their overall mobility.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the active zone tracking experiments.

claim: Automated tracking of large numbers of SVs, based on an autoregressive motion algorithm, enabled characterization of complex vesicle movements.
source: Automated tracking of large numbers of SVs, based on an autoregressive motion algorithm, enabled characterization of complex vesicle movements, complexity that could not be assessed by simple Brownian motion analysis.
evidence: This is a statement about the methodology used in the study.

claim: The diffusion coefficients calculated from MSD curves were comparable to those calculated from FRAP experiments in calyceal giant terminals.
source: In calyceal giant terminals, the diffusion coefficients calculated from MSD curves were comparable to those calculated from FRAP experiments.
evidence: This is a comparison of two different experimental methods.

claim: At least three groups of SVs with different dynamic properties and trajectories exist: intra-swelling trafficking (slow and short (S) trajectories), intermediate trafficking (moderate speed and medium (M) trajectories), and inter-swelling trafficking (fast and long (L) trajectories).
source: Our present analysis revealed at least three groups of SVs with different dynamic properties and trajectories: intra-swelling trafficking (slow and short (S) trajectories), intermediate trafficking (moderate speed and medium (M) trajectories), and inter-swelling trafficking (fast and long (L) trajectories).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the trajectory analysis.

claim: SV movements are highly heterogeneous in giant calyceals, combining both diffusional and active motions.
source: We showed that SV movements are highly heterogeneous in giant calyceals, combining both diffusional and active motions.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the displacement modality analysis.

claim: A clear, positive correlation exists between SV trajectory length and SV traveling speed.
source: Among all the individual trajectories analyzed in our study, we observed a clear, positive correlation between SV trajectory length and SV traveling speed, implying that the time required for SVs to move over short or long distances could be normalized by this mechanism.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the trajectory analysis.

claim: The time required for SVs to move over short or long distances could be normalized by the positive correlation between trajectory length and speed.
source: Among all the individual trajectories analyzed in our study, we observed a clear, positive correlation between SV trajectory length and SV traveling speed, implying that the time required for SVs to move over short or long distances could be normalized by this mechanism.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the observed correlation.

claim: SVs remote from active zones could potentially reach their release sites with the same efficiency as SVs closer to AZs.
source: This suggests that SVs remote from active zones (AZs) could potentially reach their release sites with the same efficiency as SVs closer to AZs.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the observed correlation between trajectory length and speed.

claim: Recycling SVs undergoing release at neuromuscular junctions do not have preferential spatial distributions, but are scattered randomly within nerve terminals.
source: These findings are complementary to a report showing that recycling SVs undergoing release at neuromuscular junctions do not have preferential spatial distributions, but are scattered randomly within nerve terminals (Rizzoli and Betz, 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Terminal size is one of the biological factors influencing SV mobility.
source: Thus, terminal size is clearly one of the biological factors influencing SV mobility.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the comparison of calyceal and hippocampal terminals.

claim: Discrepancies in SV mobility reported thus far might arise from differences in molecular composition of SVs between and/or within synapses.
source: Interestingly, Peng et al. (2012) suggested that discrepancies in SV mobility reported thus far might arise from differences in molecular composition of SVs between and/or within synapses.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: SV proteins are commonly divided into two classes: transport proteins and trafficking proteins.
source: SV proteins are commonly divided into two classes, based on their functions: transport proteins (proton pump, VGLUT, etc.) that mediate neurotransmitter uptake, and trafficking proteins (rab, synaptotagmin, etc.) involved in SV intracellular transport and movements (Sudhof, 1999).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: VGLUT isoforms have different regional and developmental expression.
source: VGLUT isoforms have different regional and developmental expression (Liguz-Lecznar and Skangiel-Kramska, 2007), and reportedly produce different release probabilities (Weston et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Dynamic properties of VGLUT1- and VGLUT2-expressing vesicles might result from different affinities for tethering/scaffolding proteins or molecular motors.
source: Speculatively, dynamic properties of VGLUT1- and VGLUT2-expressing vesicles might result from different affinities for tethering/scaffolding proteins or molecular motors.
evidence: This is a speculation about the mechanism underlying the observed differences.

claim: The ratio between SVs containing specific molecular markers, as well as their distribution and positioning within terminals, likely explain differences in SV mobility observed at various synapses.
source: It is likely that the ratio between SVs containing specific molecular markers, as well as their distribution and positioning within terminals, explain differences in SV mobility observed at various synapses.
evidence: This is a speculation about factors influencing SV mobility.

claim: ~15% of labeled vesicles move between presynaptic swellings at high speeds and with long, directional trajectories.
source: We have identified a large population, ~15% of labeled vesicles, moving between presynaptic swellings at high speeds and with long, directional trajectories.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data.

claim: The population of SVs undergoing inter-swelling exchange in giant calyceal terminals is three times larger than that observed in conventional-sized hippocampal synapses.
source: This population of SVs undergoing inter-swelling exchange in giant calyceal terminals appears to be three times larger than that observed in conventional-sized hippocampal synapses (Alabi and Tsien, 2012) and previously designated as the 'super pool.'
evidence: This is a comparison of experimental data to previous work.

claim: In hippocampal terminals, actin is involved in SV movements from the super pool.
source: In hippocampal terminals, actin (Darcy et al., 2006) and BDNF (Staras et al., 2010) are reportedly involved in SV movements from the super pool.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: In hippocampal terminals, BDNF is involved in SV movements from the super pool.
source: In hippocampal terminals, actin (Darcy et al., 2006) and BDNF (Staras et al., 2010) are reportedly involved in SV movements from the super pool.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: A large 'super pool' and presynaptic MTs may be required to coordinate fast and efficient cycling of SVs among the numerous release sites present in single giant terminals.
source: We speculate that a large 'super pool' and presynaptic MTs may be required to coordinate fast and efficient cycling of SVs among the numerous release sites present in single giant terminals, compared to the constitutive sharing and replenishment of SVs observed in multiple individual conventional boutons.
evidence: This is a speculation about the functional role of the super pool and MTs.

claim: Presynaptic morphology can significantly influence SV dynamics and movements.
source: Our data show that presynaptic morphology can significantly influence SV dynamics and movements.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the developmental analysis.

claim: During development, giant terminals in culture undergo significant reorganization of their presynaptic compartments.
source: During development, giant terminals in culture undergo significant reorganization of their presynaptic compartments (i.e. increased surface, volume, and complexity), leading to formation of mature synaptic connections and associated with a 1.5-fold reduction in SV dynamics and movements.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data.

claim: The high SV mobility observed in immature terminals might arise from co-transport of AZ components and other synaptic proteins with SV precursors.
source: Although we cannot exclude the possibility that other molecular mechanisms occurring during synaptic growth and maturation regulate SV movements, the high SV mobility observed in immature terminals might arise from two independent, but integrative factors: (i) co-transport of AZ components and other synaptic proteins with SV precursors (Okada et al., 1995; Yonekawa et al., 1998; Stagi et al., 2005) and (ii) changes in mechanical tension during synaptic development.
evidence: This is a speculation supported by citations to previous work.

claim: The high SV mobility observed in immature terminals might arise from changes in mechanical tension during synaptic development.
source: Although we cannot exclude the possibility that other molecular mechanisms occurring during synaptic growth and maturation regulate SV movements, the high SV mobility observed in immature terminals might arise from two independent, but integrative factors: (i) co-transport of AZ components and other synaptic proteins with SV precursors (Okada et al., 1995; Yonekawa et al., 1998; Stagi et al., 2005) and (ii) changes in mechanical tension during synaptic development.
evidence: This is a speculation about the mechanism underlying high SV mobility in immature terminals.

claim: The rise in mechanical tension associated with expansion of the presynaptic area during development could increase the probability of fast active motions.
source: On another hand, the rise in mechanical tension associated with expansion of the presynaptic area during development (Siechen et al., 2009; Ahmed et al., 2012) could increase the probability of fast active motions, as observed in Aplysia neurons (Ahmed and Saif, 2014).
evidence: This is a speculation supported by citations to previous work.

claim: After formation of stable and mature synaptic contacts, coordinated trafficking of SVs and AZ components may diminish and mechanical tensions may lessen, simultaneously reducing active transport and SV mobility.
source: After formation of stable and mature synaptic contacts during stages 3 and 4, coordinated trafficking of SVs and AZ components may diminish and mechanical tensions may lessen, simultaneously reducing active transport and SV mobility.
evidence: This is a speculation about the mechanism underlying reduced SV mobility in mature terminals.

claim: The structural organization of the MT cytoskeleton might account for the decrease in SV mobility observed between finger-like processes and swellings.
source: These factors, in addition to the structural organization of the MT cytoskeleton, might also account for the decrease (1.4 times) in SV mobility observed between finger-like processes and swellings.
evidence: This is a speculation about factors influencing SV mobility in different terminal regions.

claim: SV trafficking between endocytosis and exocytosis remain largely unchanged upon stimulation.
source: In giant calyceal terminals, neither chemical nor electrical stimulation increased SV mobility, in agreement with previous reports at the neuromuscular junction (Betz and Bewick, 1992) or at hippocampal synapses (Lemke and Klingauf, 2005; Kamin et al., 2010). These results imply that SV trafficking between endocytosis and exocytosis remain largely unchanged upon stimulation.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the stimulation experiments and comparison to previous work.

claim: SVs, undergoing exocytosis, might transiently change their mobility during stimulation.
source: However, our results do not exclude the possibility that SVs, undergoing exocytosis, might transiently change their mobility during stimulation, and image analysis at higher spatial and temporal resolution might resolve putative changes in SV movements involved in neurotransmitter release.
evidence: This is a speculation about potential changes not detected by the current methods.

claim: After KCl stimulation, SVs were immobilized near release sites.
source: Nevertheless, our analysis has revealed some alterations of SV dynamics after KCl stimulation, inducing clustering of SVs in calyeceal swellings, and a marked reduction in long trajectory SV movements. Presumably, after KCl stimulation, SVs were immobilized near release sites.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the KCl stimulation data.

claim: SVs depleted from the RRP during exocytosis were replenished from a recycling pool of SVs previously moving with active displacements.
source: Likewise, hypertonic sucrose stimulation, which depletes SVs from the RRP (Stevens and Tsujimoto, 1995) significantly reduced the number of actively moving SVs, suggesting that SVs depleted from the RRP during exocytosis were replenished from a recycling pool of SVs previously moving with active displacements.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the sucrose stimulation data and a citation to previous work.

claim: Direct support of synaptic transmission might be provided by fast diffusive and subtle local changes in SV mobility near release sites.
source: Direct support of synaptic transmission might be provided by fast diffusive and subtle local changes in SV mobility near release sites as recently reported (Rothman et al., 2016), rather than diverse and heterogenous SV movements prior to release.
evidence: This is a speculation supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: Diverse and heterogenous SV movements prior to release may contribute to distribute SVs in optimal locations for the functional and structural maintenance of presynaptic terminals.
source: The latter may contribute to distribute SVs in optimal locations for the functional and structural maintenance of presynaptic terminals.
evidence: This is a speculation about the functional role of heterogeneous SV movements.

claim: Newly endocytosed SVs had low mobility with their distribution confined near endocytic regions for the first hour.
source: In this regard, during the process of SV labeling, newly endocytosed SVs had low mobility with their distribution confined near endocytic regions for the first hour.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data.

claim: Low SV mobility near exo/endocytic regions is likely caused by tethering of SVs around release sites.
source: Low SV mobility near exo/endocytic regions is likely caused by tethering of SVs around release sites.
evidence: This is a speculation about the mechanism underlying low SV mobility near exo/endocytic regions.

claim: Synapsin-1 is thought to tether SVs in its dephosphorylated form.
source: Classically, synapsin-1 is thought to tether SVs in its dephosphorylated form (Llinás et al., 1985).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: OA increases SV mobility by ~10 times in hippocampal terminals.
source: The broad-spectrum phosphatase inhibitor OA increases SV mobility by ~10 times in hippocampal terminals (Jordan et al., 2005) or at the neuromuscular junction (Gaffield et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: OA increases SV mobility by ~10 times at the neuromuscular junction.
source: The broad-spectrum phosphatase inhibitor OA increases SV mobility by ~10 times in hippocampal terminals (Jordan et al., 2005) or at the neuromuscular junction (Gaffield et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work.

claim: In calyceal terminals, OA only increased SV mobility by ~1.4 times, suggesting higher abundancy of untethered SVs in these terminals and/or phosphorylation independent SV tethering.
source: In calyceal terminals, OA only increased SV mobility by ~1.4 times, similar to that recently reported at cerebellar mossy fiber terminals (~2 times; Rothman et al., 2016), suggesting higher abundancy of untethered SVs in these terminals and/or phosphorylation independent SV tethering with molecules such as Basson (Hallermann et al., 2010) or Unc analogs (Böhme et al., 2016).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the OA treatment data and comparison to previous work.

claim: SV movements and supply can be influenced by morphological characteristics of presynaptic terminals and by molecular signatures of vesicles.
source: Altogether, our data indicate that in central nervous system, SV movements are highly heterogenous and that large synapses possess higher basal SV mobility than smaller synapses. Our results also suggest that SV movements and supply can be influenced by morphological characteristics of presynaptic terminals and by molecular signatures of vesicles.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the overall experimental data.

claim: Presynaptic morphology and vesicular composition appeared to be major biological determinants characterizing SV dynamics and trafficking in central synapses.
source: Although the underlying molecular mechanisms remain to be characterized, presynaptic morphology and vesicular composition appeared to be major biological determinants characterizing SV dynamics and trafficking in central synapses.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the overall experimental data.
